summary: The market splits into five clusters, none of which occupies know-expand's exact position. (1) Document-grounded study tools: Google NotebookLM (17M+ MAU, free to $99.99-200/mo via Google AI tiers, added its own Deep Research in Nov 2025 plus audio/video/slide outputs) and Anara/ex-Unriddle (claims 3M users, $10-20/mo, $167/mo Deep Search, passage-level citation verification). These produce interactive artifacts or short reports, never long verified documents. (2) Foundation-lab Deep Research features (OpenAI $20/$100/$200 tiers with 10/50/250 runs per month, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity at $20/mo with 45M users and ~$450M ARR): commodity 10-40 page web-sourced reports, no pedagogy, no verification pass, no bibliographic rigor. (3) Scientific literature tools: Elicit (2M+ users, $12-79/user/mo plus custom enterprise, PRISMA 2020 systematic-review product for pharma), Consensus (10M+ users, $30M Series A May 2026, $10-45/mo), SciSpace ($12-20/mo), Undermind ($16-20/mo, YC, 1,000+ GSK scientists), and Ai2's free open-source Asta agents on Semantic Scholar — these do search/screening/extraction, not synthesis into learning material. (4) Open source: Stanford STORM (70k preview users, short Wikipedia-style articles, research artifact) and gpt-researcher (27.4k GitHub stars, 5-10 page reports). (5) The closest analog on depth and pricing: Edison Scientific's Kosmos ($70M seed at $250M valuation; 12-hour autonomous runs reading ~1,500 papers producing fully-cited reports at $200/run) — but it targets discovery/hypothesis generation, not pedagogy. AI doc-to-course L&D tools (Coassemble, eduMe, Synthesia, eSkilled at $9-29/mo) produce shallow microlearning from internal docs, and Google's Learn Your Way/LearnLM personalizes existing textbooks rather than creating field guides from papers. WHITE SPACE: no product combines (a) 200+ page book-grade artifact, (b) citation verification/audit, (c) pedagogical structuring (reader profiling, prerequisites, worked examples), (d) seeded from one paper. Nobody is paying for that exact artifact yet because nobody sells it — but adjacent segments pay heavily for verified synthesized documents: pharma spends ~$141k per systematic literature review (~$16.8M/yr per top-10 pharma company); AlphaSense hit $600M ARR at a $7.5B valuation (June 2026) selling verified research synthesis to 7,000 enterprises; Hebbia ($161M raised) penetrated 33% of top asset managers for diligence document synthesis; expert networks are a ~$3B market growing toward ~$4.9B; corporate training is a $400B market with AI-powered training at $7.49B in 2026 and Sana (acquired by Workday) charging $50-100k/yr; Primer ($237M raised) sells traceable synthesis to defense/intel; and OpenEvidence ($12B valuation, used by 40%+ of US physicians) proves that citation-grounded domain synthesis can reach massive adoption when verification is the headline feature. The risk: deep-research output is commoditizing fast (NotebookLM bundling at $7.99/mo), so the defensible position is the verified, typeset, pedagogically-structured book — priced per artifact (Kosmos validates $200/run), sold into pharma medical affairs, consulting/PE technical diligence, defense/intel, and technical onboarding rather than to individual learners.

NotebookLM added its own Deep Research mode on Nov 13, 2025 (agentic web research compiled into citation-backed reports added as notebook sources), followed by Gemini 3 upgrade, PPTX export, and 1M-token chat through early 2026
ChatGPT Deep Research quotas are tiered: Plus $20/mo gets 10 runs/month, Pro $100/mo gets 50, Pro $200/mo gets 250 — output is a report, not a structured learning artifact

Consensus raised a $30M Series A in May 2026, has 10M+ users and 170+ university library partnerships; pricing Free / Pro $10 / Deep $45 per month
SciSpace (ex-Typeset) prices at Free / $12/mo Premium / $20/user/mo Teams / $100/mo Lab over a 280M-paper index — summarization and copilot, no long-form synthesis
Undermind (YC-backed, ~$500K raised) charges ~$16-20/mo Pro for deep adaptive literature search; used by 1,000+ scientists at GSK plus MIT/Harvard/Caltech/Princeton researchers
Ai2's Asta (launched Aug 2025) is a free, open-source agentic research platform grounded in Semantic Scholar's 200M+ papers — commoditizing literature-search infrastructure rather than monetizing it
Stanford STORM generates short Wikipedia-style cited articles; 70,000+ people tried the research preview but it remains an unmonetized academic project
gpt-researcher has ~27,400 GitHub stars (May 2026) and produces free multi-source cited reports — open-source baseline for the 'deep research report' commodity

Edison Scientific (FutureHouse spinout, $70M seed at $250M valuation, Nov 2025) sells Kosmos: 12-hour autonomous runs reading ~1,500 papers producing fully-cited research reports at $200/run after 6 free academic runs — the strongest pricing comp for a per-artifact deep synthesis product

Anara (ex-Unriddle, YC) claims 3M+ researchers; $10-30/mo tiers plus a $167/mo Deep Search tier; differentiates on passage-level citation verification where every claim links to the exact source sentence

Each pharma systematic literature review costs ~$141,195 in manual labor; top-10 pharma companies each publish ~119 SLRs/year (~$16.8M/yr per company) — the clearest evidence of six-figure willingness to pay for verified synthesized documents

AlphaSense raised $350M at a $7.5B valuation in June 2026, surpassing $600M ARR with 7,000+ enterprise customers (70%+ of S&P 500) and now ships its own Deep Research product over 500M premium business documents
Hebbia ($161M raised, $700M valuation) penetrated 33% of top global asset managers for M&A diligence and investment-memo document synthesis
Expert networks (synthesized expert knowledge for consulting/PE) were a ~$3B market in 2025 growing ~12%/yr toward ~$4.9B in 2026, with consulting at ~50% of spend

Corporate training is a ~$400B market; AI-powered corporate training is $7.49B in 2026 (19.4% CAGR); Sana Labs ($136M raised, acquired by Workday Sept 2025) charged $50-100k/yr enterprise contracts — but doc-to-course tools (Coassemble, eduMe, Synthesia, $9-29/mo) only produce shallow microlearning

Primer AI ($237M raised, incl. $69M in Dec 2025) sells traceable summarization/knowledge-discovery to defense and intelligence agencies and Fortune 50 companies — provenance is the purchase criterion in this segment

OpenEvidence reached a $12B valuation (Jan 2026, $250M Series D) with 40%+ of US physicians using it and $100M+ revenue — proof that citation-grounded, verified domain synthesis wins massive adoption when trust is the headline feature

Google's Learn Your Way (LearnLM, Google Labs) converts existing textbooks into adaptive multi-format learning material and showed RCT gains — validating pedagogy-aware generation, but it does not create field guides from papers

implications: The exact artifact know-expand produces — a 200+ page verified, pedagogically-structured, typeset field guide grown from one seed paper — has no direct competitor. Every adjacent tool stops at either short reports (Deep Research, STORM, gpt-researcher), interactive study aids (NotebookLM, Anara), search/extraction (Elicit, Consensus, Undermind, Asta), or discovery reports (Kosmos). The white space is real, but so is the reason it's empty: no proven consumer demand for book-length output, so validation must come from professional segments.

Do not price as a $10-20/mo subscription — that band is saturated (NotebookLM $7.99, Consensus $10, Elicit $12, SciSpace $12, Undermind $16, Perplexity/ChatGPT/Anara $20) and buys commodity reports. Kosmos's $200/run and Anara's $167/mo Deep Search tier validate per-artifact / premium pricing; a verified 200-page guide plausibly supports $100-500 per run, which also comfortably covers know-expand's token costs (relevant to the planned --batch-mode 50% discount).

Verification is the marketable moat, not generation. Anara wins users with passage-level citation links; OpenEvidence reached a $12B valuation on citation-grounded trust; Primer sells traceability to defense. know-expand's S8 citation audit, CSL-JSON bibliography, 65/35 foundational/frontier split, and [NEEDS_CITATION] discipline should be the headline of any positioning — and surfacing a per-claim 'verification report' alongside the PDF would make the moat visible.

The S1 interview and S3 human taxonomy review are differentiators, not friction: Google's Learn Your Way RCT showed personalization to the reader measurably improves outcomes, and no deep-research competitor profiles the reader at all. Keep human-in-the-loop as a premium feature rather than racing the fully-autonomous tools.

Best-paying wedges in order of evidence strength: (1) pharma medical affairs / literature review teams (~$141k per SLR, $16.8M/yr per top-10 pharma; Elicit Enterprise proves the buyer exists — a PRISMA-adjacent 'field guide' mode could ride the same budget); (2) consulting/PE technical due diligence (AlphaSense $600M ARR, Hebbia in 33% of top asset managers — a deep-tech diligence guide from a target's key patent/paper is a natural fit); (3) defense/intel analyst onboarding (Primer's segment; know-expand's provenance/event-log architecture fits the traceability requirement); (4) corporate technical onboarding L&D ($50-100k/yr Sana-style contracts; existing doc-to-course tools are shallow, leaving deep technical material unserved).

Commoditization is the main threat and it is fast: NotebookLM shipped Deep Research, 1M-token chat, and PPTX export within ~5 months and bundles at $7.99/mo. know-expand should not market itself as 'deep research' (a lost battle) but as 'the verified book' — output quality (xelatex typesetting, prerequisite primers, worked examples, boss-node synthesis) that chat products structurally won't replicate.

Free infrastructure is improving in know-expand's favor: Ai2's Asta/Semantic Scholar (already used for bibliography) and OpenAlex (already used for taxonomy validation) are open and grounded — the cost structure of the pipeline benefits while competitors who monetize search (Consensus, Undermind) get squeezed.

GTM pattern worth copying from Edison/Kosmos: a small free tier of full runs (they give 6 to academics) to let the artifact sell itself, since a 200-page verified guide is a demo that no screenshot conveys; pair with per-run pricing for individuals and seat/volume licensing for the pharma/consulting/defense segments.
